May I point out to the
hon. gentleman that such a course is not now practicable. These are estimates of the requirements of expenditure for the public service during the coming year. When the treasury board and the government as a whole finally formulated these estimates they took into consideration the reductions, the total amounting, as the right hon. leader of the opposition has said, to some $40,000,000. Included in those reductions was the anticipated reduction of 10 per cent in the salary. Now, then, the whole of the estimates are based upon that expectation, and they are presented to parliament accordingly. The only way in which we could now make a change would be to introduce by resolution an additional estimate covering the amounts that are left out of the present estimates affecting the salaries of the civil service. In other words, it would require a supplementary estimate. I would suggest to my hon. friend so far as the resolution that is now before us is concerned-and the same argument will apply to many others-that its adoption does not in itself affect the salary of anyone. But when I am asked: Is it the intention of the government out of the vote to pay the same salary as that paid last year? I am bound to say: No, what the government intends to do is to make a cut, subject of course to parliament approving of such a procedure. The adoption of this resolution, I repeat, does not make a cut in anybody's salary at all.

We accept the principle of
it.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

The adoption of the
resolution certainly does not accept the principle in the face of the discussion we have had. Everybody now knows there is a sharp cleavage of opinion regarding that principle.
Mr. RALSTON. It means the ministry will not have enough money except to pay reduced salaries.

We would have to cut
out travelling expenses for instance. Let me make it quite clear that the adoption of this resolution would not in any way affect the salary of a single person; we have enough money in the vote to pay the salaries of those employed on administration of gas and electricity.
With 10 per cent off.

With 10 per cent on. If
parliament does not by statute approve of what the Prime Minister has announced, then the only way in which proper effect could be given to these estimates as they are would be to bring in supplementary estimates to make up whatever reductions are contained in these estimates, because otherwise so far as this vote ' is concerned other parts of the service would be short of funds.

Could it not be corrected by passing the estimates under the old salary schedule, without the statutory increases, and then let the Prime Minister bring in his bill to provide for the 10 per cent cut?-

I have already tried to
make clear that so far as this resolution is concerned its acceptance does not affect anybody's salary.
But it is going to put them on that basis.

The appropriation for
salaries, travelling expenses, purchase of equipment and contingencies would raise the vote to what we think is necessary. To run the whole branch would mean a supplementary estimate. We could not run it on this vote.

To pay the
same salaries as last year?

Yes, to carry out the
whole thing.

Having regard to what the minister has just said about it not being practicable to meet this involved situation in the way suggested, and having regard also to what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) stated a moment ago, might 41761-181
I now ask the ministry if the shortest as well as the proper course would not be to bring in at once the bill which the Prime Minister has promised authorizing the 10 per cent reduction? The Minister of Justice said the bill would be a short one-that he could tell us at once what it would be; it would be in two clauses.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I said it would validate whatever it was necessary to validate.

As I understood it there would be two main provisions, one, to use his exact words, to legalize what we do in the estimates, and the other to authorize the 10 per cent reduction. Those phrases are enlightening as well as interesting. "To legalize what we do in the estimates"-in other words, it is recognized that certain things we are being asked to do will later have to be legalized. I do not think we ought to be asked to do anything in the interim which is not strictly legal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The estimates state that.

Whether or not it is so stated, I do not think it is the correct way for parliament to proceed. In time of war many things were done which were illegal. They were legalized later in time of peace, when parliament was asked to pass measures to that effect, but there is no need to resort to war measures in times of peace, and at a time like this, I think we would do well to make a special effort to 'hold to the constitutional method oif procedure. Why should not the government bring in that bill immediately? It will be short, and will provide an immediate means of settling this question.
The Minister of Justice suggested again what the Minister of Finance suggested a while ago, that the opposition might bring in a motion on going into supply and have the matter discussed at that time. I made it clear a short time ago that we did not intend to proceed in that way, for the reason that any motion brought forward on going into supply would be construed by the ministry as a want of confidence motion and, as such, would offer to the followers of the ministry an excuse for not asserting their point of view in regard to this matter. We do not intend to afford them that means of escape.
The simplest way is for the ministry to introduce at once the bill authorizing the ten per cent reduction. Let us discuss that bill and when it is passed, if it is passed, the ministry will have authority to do what they are now proposing to do in the estimates. If

Supply-Trade and Commerce
it is not passed, or if it is modified, the estimates will have to be altered in accordance with the will of parliament. That would be the quickest way and, I think, the only regular way of proceeding.

I had some rather extensive remarks to make on this subject. As the house has rightly assumed I am opposed io these cuts, but in view of the remarks of the Minister of Justice I will defer my statement until a later date. I suppose I shall have an opportunity on some of the other items. I am doing this because of the statement of the Minister of Justice, who at present is leading the house, that no requests have been received by the government for an opportunity for associations of civil servants to present their point of view. I desire to afford an opportunity to those vitally concerned in this matter to consider whether or not they desire to be heard by the government and to decide whether they will ask to be heard. When these items come up, if that opportunity has not been afforded them after they have asked for it, I will avail myself of the opportunity of saying what I desire to say in this regard.

I do not propose to enter into a constitutional debate at this hour of the night. So far as I am concerned I believe the Minister of Finance, speaking for the government, stated the fact when he said they had proceeded in the constitutional manner, the manner which has been established as the regular procedure year by year. But it was also stated by the Minister of Justice that his object was to provide the most convenient method of disposing of this question, the method following the line of common sense and creating the least disturbance to the house.
I would suggest as a matter of convenience, Mr. Chairman, and in order to save as much time as possible, that we should decide upon this principle first. The principle of the cut is an unusual one, and while we are following ordinary rules of procedure at present we must admit that this is not a usual situation. Every item is predicated upon this 10 per cent cut, and we cannot discuss any item without also discussing this question, upon which obviously there is some difference of opinion as to the extent of the cut and as to the question of a graduated reduction in the lower salaries.
It does seem to me that it would save a great deal of time and avoid perhaps a hundred disjointed and sectional debates if we could decide first upon the principle upon

which these items are predicated and then, in the light of that discussion, consider the estimates with some degree of intelligence and coolness. The Minister of Finance stated that it would be a matter of some difficulty to provide a method by which this might be done, and he said this was the only method. I think he was not doing justice to the ingenuity, if not the wisdom, of the government itself. I am under the impression that if the government is desirous of ascertaining the opinion of the house upon this matter, and doing it before we enter upon the discussion of these items affected by the 10 per cent cut, it could be done very well either by adopting the suggestion of the right hon. leader of the opposition and introducing at once the bill which is to legalize the whole matter, or by way of a resolution asking the house for a free expression of opinion as to the principle upon which all the estimates are based, before the estimates themselves are considered item by item. I think that would be the fairest method, and in the end it would not only save time but also would save a great many tempers which had better be kept for some more useful purpose.

There is one point I should like the minister to clear up. The Prime Minister stated that the 10 per cent reduction would apply to all civil servants except the judges, who he said were in a somewhat different position. Hundreds of thousands of dollars are required to pay our judges, who get fair salaries and receive pensions and so on. If I vote in favour of a resolution which cuts by 10 per cent the salary of a civil servant receiving $1,000 or $1,200, and then speak and vote against the bill if it does not include the judges, in what position would that leave me?

In adopting this resolution my hon. friend is not voting for a cut in the salary of any employee. As I said on two or three previous occasions to-night, the amount provided here is in expectation of a cut, but by the act of voting this resolution no cut is made, and no cut can be made without further action or further measures.
But the item is predicated upon the cut.
Quite so; I have stated to the committee that the provision of the amount is predicated upon the expectation that there will be a cut.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said quite often that by adopting these estimates we are not admitting the principle of a 10 per cent cut. Early

Supply-Trade and Commerce
in the evening he decided to allow the civil government estimates to stand because they had to do entirely with salaries. Looking through all the estimates I find the words "less 10 per cent" more frequently than I find anything else. If this discussion had not taken place I could imagine what the Prime Minister would have said when he presented his bill. He would have said, "Why, you admitted the principle when you passed the estimates that have gone through committee."
I could hear him say that, and deny us the right even to discuss the question because we admitted the 10 per cent reduction in salaries in connection with some of the public works estimates this afternoon, as the minister has said. Following the suggestion of my leader, I think we had better discuss the subject, and the government would be well advised to do so right now.

I think the minister himself is now convinced that he has approached this question in the wrong way. Hon. gentlemen sitting to your left, Mr. Chairman, went about the country a couple of years ago and told about the prosperous times they were going to usher in, but they are not standing up now for the working man; instead they are reducing salaries. The minister will agree that those of us who oppose this reduction in salaries and wages will have to scrutinize every item. We shall have to ascertain certain things before we can tell just what we are voting. We shall have to ask how many employees are affected under every item, how many years of service they have put in, how many of them are denied statutory increases, whether some are being affected to the extent of 10 or 15 per cent, and so on. I submit * that this is an occasion on which the Minister of Labour ought to be in his place to suggest a board of conciliation and investigation into the question. But there is one thing I want to ask the minister and the leader of the government. It is quite evident to me that the senior member for Ottawa has not the full purport of the answers given both by the Minister of Justice and by the minister in charge of the estimates. In effect, he asked whether time would be given for the representatives of the civil service as a whole to make their representations to the government before the reduction went into force. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he would never close his door to any in his department. Is that an answer to the senior member for Ottawa? The Minister of Justice also tried to evade that particular question. Where, I ask, is the national council of the civil service which was established in
1929? When we passed an order in council establishing the civil service council it was for the purpose of enabling them to discuss with the government precisely such questions as the one now before us. We provided in the estimates to bring representatives of the civil service from all over Canada, and this government has ignored that provision entirely. So that there is no civil service council in this country to-day, or else it is entirely ignored. What would you say of a private employer of labour who would attempt a reduction of from 10 to 15 per cent in the wages of his employees-because that is what it amounts to in many instances-without giving the representatives of the working men an opportunity of discussing the question with him? Yet that is what this government is doing. It is no wonder the Minister of Trade and Commerce rose with some heat a little while ago. I remember how solicitous he was, when on this side of the house, for the poor underpaid civil servants, charging the present leader of the opposition with an attempt to stir up heat and discontent in the country. One of the gentlemen who went through the country in July, 1930, stirring up strife and trouble everywhere made a laughing stock of the old age pensions legislation, misrepresenting the whole thing. Indeed, the party supporting him organized unemployed gangs throughout the country and put white labels upon them so that they would give an inkling to the people of how many unemployed there were in the country. They got them to attend meetings and cheer government candidates. Now the hon. gentleman gets up and tells the leader of the opposition that he is trying to stir up trouble, and when anyone tries to make a sensible suggestion-
Oh, oh.

-he sits snarling. Hon. gentlemen laugh; no one will suppose that those on the other side are competent to judge what is a sensible suggestion. When a sensible suggestion is offered to the other side or to the minister he snarls in his seat and yells, "nonsense." I should say, judging by the number of times that he has emitted that word "nonsense," he is not the best judge of what is sense. What I want to know is this: Is this government going to reduce the salaries of civil servants in Canada without giving the representatives of these people, men, women and girls, an opportunity' to present their views? That is what I want to know. Personally I am prepared to stay here until the snow flies next year rather than pass these estimates under these conditions.

The Minister of Trade and
Commerce made the statement at least two or three times that if the committee passed this vote of $211,000 and if afterwards, when the government brought down legislation providing for the reduction of 10 per cent, that legislation was not endorsed by the house, it would not affect the salaries included in this vote. The minister was asked to give the details of this $211,000, and Hansard tomorrow morning will show that he itemized the different amounts necessary to make the total of this vote, less $37,600. In other words, the minister's total for the different detailed items, if I remember correctly, was $247,000, or $248,000, which included, in addition to the $202,000 in salaries, certain other items. Now the minister comes along and says that if this legislation does not pass when it is introduced it will not affect the salaries included in this item. But he told us that in this $211,000 we are voting there are certain other amounts. Surely that $37,600 of a reduction means something, and the other items outside of salaries which we vote now in this item cannot be touched to pay salaries if the legislation is not passed. I would ask the minister for a detailed account of that $37,600, and I have no hesitation in saying before he replies that part of that $37,600 is the 10 per cent deduction from the $240,000 odd.

My hon. friend perhaps
forgot or did not hear me say that unquestionably, if such legislation as I have intimated were not passed in statutory form, making the cut of 10 per cent, it would be necessary for us to bring in a supplementary to make up the difference. What I was trying [DOT] to impress upon the committee was this. I do not say for one moment that this vote provides for the present range of salaries and all other requirements of the branch. What I did say was that by the passing of this resolution you were not cutting salaries. I told the committee at the very outset on introducing the vote that it was intended that the vote should be sufficient, with the cut in salary. I made that statement frankly and clearly. We are providing in this vote for a certain sum of money which contemplates the cut of 10 per cent in salary. There is no question that by the passing of the resolution we do not actually make the cut.

I cannot understand the hon.
minister's argument, because when we asked for an itemized statement he told us that this vote included other items besides salaries.
Surely.

The minister agrees. He then comes along and tells the committee that if the legislation to implement the cut does not pass the salaries will not be affected, that he will ask for an extra vote in the supplementary estimates. The minister forgets that he is asking the committee not only to pass this item of $202,000 for salaries, less $37,600, but also to pass several other items which go to make up that total. For instance, at the end of March not only will the salaries have to be paid but one-twelfth of the other amounts will have to be paid. Does the minister mean to say that he is going to pay the salaries and leave unpaid the other amounts should this committee defeat this item? The minister is not on solid ground. It is plain to everyone that the salaries included in this item will be reduced to the tune of 10 per cent.
The Auditor General would not permit the conversion of one amount to the benefit of another.

My hon. friend must
understand that before this vote becomes effective, which will not be until the end of March, the necessary legislation will have been introduced and passed.

My hon. friend said in his
argument that it might not pass.
No, I did not.
If it should not pass.

If it should not pass. It has been stated by the Prime Minister and was stated to-night by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice that unquestionably it is contemplated that legislation will be introduced. We recognize the objection of hon. gentlemen opposite to dealing with these votes until that legislation has been disposed of. That is a position which they are entitled to take and we do not quarrel with it. But what we have tried to do is to explain to the committee the precise grounds upon which these estimates have been prepared. They state clearly and frankly what should be and should not be provided for, and they have been offered to the house in that way. What has occurred in connection with this vote will occur in connection with many others. Perhaps I could pick out one or two votes in which no salaries are involved, but there would not be very many. These estimates have been prepared in contemplation of the cut in salaries, and it is intended that legislation supplementing that intention or, as the Minister of Justice has said, making provision to legalize the cut, will be introduced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Whatever may be the
view of others, I do not think the evening has been wasted. I believe that the suggestions made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie Ring) and by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) are worthy of consideration. If a discussion of the 10 per cent cut is to take place on every item, the debate would be interminable. The only object of the government has been to meet the convenience of the house, not to prejudice the position of any hon. member who is entitled to express his views and record his vote as he sees fit.
I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I agree with what the
minister has said, but I would point out that it was the Minister of Finance who said that this matter must be discussed right now.
